context_blurb:
Kick a ball across a field and it soon rolls to a stop. For centuries most thinkers took that as proof that moving things need a push to keep going. Finding out why they were wrong gave us Isaac Newton's first law of motion, the law of inertia, at work every time a car brakes or turns.

The Greek philosopher Aristotle taught that things on Earth come to rest once nothing keeps them moving. Galileo Galilei tested that for himself. He rolled bronze balls along grooved wooden ramps, timing them with a water clock. A ball run down one ramp and on up a facing one rises nearly to the height where it began, however steep or gentle the far slope. Then Galileo imagined laying the second ramp flat and making it perfectly smooth. The ball could never climb back to its old height, so he concluded it would roll on forever at the same speed. Real balls stop because friction, the rubbing force between surfaces, and the air push against them; a ball on grass stops far sooner than one on smooth ice.

In his Dialogue of 1632, Galileo argued that a stone dropped from the top of a smoothly sailing ship's mast lands at its foot, not behind it, because the stone was already moving forward with the ship. Toss a ball straight up in a train running smoothly on a straight track, and the same thing happens: the ball keeps the train's forward speed and comes back down into your hand.

Isaac Newton made this a law in his Principia of 1687. His first law says that a thing at rest stays at rest, and a moving thing keeps moving at a steady speed in a straight line, unless an unbalanced force, one not cancelled by another, acts on it. Inertia, from the Latin word for idleness, is that resistance to any change in motion; it is a property of matter, not a force. Far out between the stars, a space probe with its engines off has almost no force acting on it, so it keeps moving straight on at the same speed. Only a force, such as a rocket firing or a planet's pull, could change that.

How much inertia a thing has depends on its mass, the amount of matter in it, so a small iron weight is far harder to start than a big beach ball full of air. A NASA lesson pictures an astronaut struggling to push a one-ton satellite out of a space shuttle's cargo bay: weightless in orbit, it still has a ton of mass. So aboard a space station, where nothing registers on a scale, whichever floating object holds more mass is still the harder one to start drifting.

When a driver brakes hard, the brakes slow only the car, so an unbelted passenger's body goes on moving at the old speed until the dashboard or the windshield stops it. A seat belt slows him with the car, spreading the force across his hips and shoulder. When a car swings left, a box on the seat keeps going in a straight line while the car turns beneath it, so the right-hand door swings round to meet it. The outward push passengers seem to feel on a bend is not a real force. A ball whirled on a string circles only because the string pulls it toward the centre. If the string snaps, the ball flies off in a straight line, the way it was heading at that instant, along the edge of the circle.

In the old tablecloth trick, a performer jerks a silk cloth from under a table set with dishes, and they stay put. The cloth does rub on the dishes the whole time it slides, but a sharp yank is over so quickly that friction has too little time to get them moving, and their inertia keeps them almost where they stood. A slow pull gives friction time to drag them along. Try it small: lay a card across a cup with a coin on top, flick the card sharply away, and the coin drops into the cup. To tighten a loose hammer head, a carpenter bangs the end of the handle down hard on the floor, head up. The handle stops short, but the head, with only the wood's friction to hold it back, keeps going and slides farther on, wedging itself tighter.
